claims.source: Our results suggest that homeostatic regulation of global responses is mediated through changes to intrinsic network-correlated inputs rather than changes to identified sensory inputs thought to drive sensory processing.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Homeostatic regulation of neuronal firing levels is a critical feature of neural circuits.
claims.source: Homeostatic regulation of neuronal firing levels is a critical feature of neural circuits.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus.

claims.claim: Homeostatic regulation allows for prolonged stable function during changing activity levels associated with ongoing Hebbian plasticity, changes in sensory drive or input loss.
claims.source: It allows for prolonged stable function during changing activity levels associated with ongoing Hebbian plasticity, changes in sensory drive or input loss (Keck et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Impairment of homeostatic regulation is thought to result in prolonged periods of excessive neuronal hyper- or hypoactivity.
claims.source: The impairment of homeostatic regulation is thought to result in prolonged periods of excessive neuronal hyper- or hypoactivity, which may impair network function (Frere and Slutsky, 2018; Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2014; Marder and Prinz, 2002; Tetzlaff et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2020; Zenke et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Homeostatic regulation occurs through plastic changes to a broad range of synaptic, intrinsic, cellular, and network-level properties.
claims.source: Homeostatic regulation occurs through plastic changes to a broad range of synaptic, intrinsic, cellular, and network-level properties (Barnes et al., 2015; Bridi et al., 2020; Bridi et al., 2018; Gainey and Feldman, 2017; Joseph and Turrigiano, 2017; Keck et al., 2017; Lee and Kirkwood, 2019; Ma et al., 2019; Turrigiano, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Homeostatic changes must facilitate rebalancing of activity while maintaining the underlying circuits established for ongoing sensory processing.
claims.source: These changes must facilitate rebalancing of activity while maintaining the underlying circuits established for ongoing sensory processing (Chen et al., 2013a; Iacaruso et al., 2017), as well as for learned (Jurjut et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2020; Poort et al., 2015) and innate behaviors (Branco and Redgrave, 2020; Evans et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Previous work in adult animals has shown that synaptic homeostatic changes occur in only a subset of synapses.
claims.source: Previous work in adult animals has shown that synaptic homeostatic changes occur in only a subset of synapses (Barnes et al., 2017) or via additive changes (Goel and Lee, 2007), as opposed to multiplicative changes across the entire population described for some homeostatic mechanisms during development and the critical period (Desai et al., 2002; Kaneko et al., 2008; Turrigiano, 2017; Turrigiano et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Sensory cortices in adult mice are multimodal and receive multiple sensory inputs.
claims.source: Sensory cortices in adult mice are known to be multimodal and receive multiple sensory inputs (Ibrahim et al., 2016; Iurilli et al., 2012; Knöpfel et al., 2019; Todd et al., 2016; Vann et al., 2009; Yoshitake et al., 2013), as well as intrinsic contextual and intracortical inputs (Fiser et al., 2016; Khan and Hofer, 2018; Miller et al., 2014; Okun et al., 2015; Pakan et al., 2016; Pakan et al., 2018b; Petrus et al., 2015; Roth et al., 2016; Saleem et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Large populations of neurons in visual cortex have a strong correlation or coupling with the average network activity.
claims.source: Large populations of neurons in visual cortex have a strong correlation or coupling with the average network activity, which is thought to be largely non-sensory and represent contextual input that may be associated with behavioral state (Okun et al., 2015; Stringer et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: High levels of network coupling are correlated with a higher probability of local intracortical connections between neurons.
claims.source: High levels of network coupling are correlated with a higher probability of local intracortical connections between neurons (Okun et al., 2015) and could also reflect the presence of other common non-sensory inputs (Yoshimura et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Chronic two-photon imaging in awake adult mice expressing GCaMP6s was used to examine the functional properties of dendritic spines.
claims.source: We used chronic two-photon imaging in awake adult mice expressing the genetically encoded calcium indicator GCaMP6s (see Methods) to examine the functional properties of dendritic spines that undergo functional plasticity following sensory deprivation.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claims.claim: Functional calcium signals in dendritic spines were repeatedly measured on the distal tufts (in layer 2/3) of layer 5 pyramidal cells in primary monocular visual cortex before and after sensory deprivation via enucleation of the contralateral eye.
claims.source: Over a span of 4 days, we repeatedly measured functional calcium signals in dendritic spines on the distal tufts (in layer 2/3) of layer 5 pyramidal cells in primary monocular visual cortex before and after sensory deprivation via enucleation of the contralateral eye (Figure 1A–C; Barnes et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methodology and references Figure 1.

claims.claim: Approximately 20% of spines in the contralateral visual cortex became inactive 12 hr after monocular deprivation.
claims.source: Consistent with previous work (Barnes et al., 2017), we found that approximately 20% of spines in the contralateral visual cortex became inactive 12 hr after monocular deprivation, with the number of inactive spines decreasing over time (Figure 1D, see Methods).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, consistent with previous work.

claims.claim: The number of inactive spines decreased over time following monocular deprivation.
claims.source: Consistent with previous work (Barnes et al., 2017), we found that approximately 20% of spines in the contralateral visual cortex became inactive 12 hr after monocular deprivation, with the number of inactive spines decreasing over time (Figure 1D, see Methods).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Persistent spines increased their functional response amplitudes on average.
claims.source: On average, the persistent (active at all time points) spines increased their functional response amplitudes (Figure 1E–F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The increased amplitude of spine responses was blocked by an intraperitoneal injection of a dominant negative form of TNF-α.
claims.source: The increased amplitude of spine responses was blocked by an intraperitoneal injection of a dominant negative form of TNF-α (Figure 1A and F), suggesting this effect is dependent on TNF-α.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data showing the effect of TNF-α inhibition.

claims.claim: The spine response amplitude increase following deprivation is dependent on TNF-α.
claims.source: The increased amplitude of spine responses was blocked by an intraperitoneal injection of a dominant negative form of TNF-α (Figure 1A and F), suggesting this effect is dependent on TNF-α.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental result that TNF-α inhibition blocks the amplitude increase.

claims.claim: Following deprivation, there were no changes over time in the average frequency of responses at the population level.
claims.source: Following deprivation, we found no changes over time in the average frequency of responses at the population level (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claims.claim: There was no correlation between changes in frequency and amplitude within individual spines.
claims.source: We observed no correlation between changes in frequency and amplitude within individual spines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), indicating that the changes in frequency are not likely to be driving the changes in amplitude within a single spine.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: Changes in frequency are not likely to be driving the changes in amplitude within a single spine.
claims.source: We observed no correlation between changes in frequency and amplitude within individual spines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), indicating that the changes in frequency are not likely to be driving the changes in amplitude within a single spine.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between frequency and amplitude changes.

claims.claim: Not all spines undergo a TNF-α-dependent strengthening following deprivation.
claims.source: We have previously used structural imaging of spine size as an in vivo proxy for synaptic strength and shown that not all spines undergo a TNF-α-dependent strengthening following deprivation (Barnes et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Spines with the lowest visual responsiveness prior to deprivation underwent the strongest functional strengthening after deprivation.
claims.source: When we examined the functional strengthening of all of the spines, we found an inverse relationship, such that the spines with the lowest visual responsiveness prior to deprivation underwent the strongest functional strengthening after deprivation (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: Only a subset of spines increased their functional responses following deprivation.
claims.source: Consistent with our previous work (Barnes et al., 2017), we observed that only a subset of spines increased their functional responses (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, consistent with previous work.

claims.claim: A majority of spines that were responsive to the sparse noise stimulus also responded to drifting gratings (97%).
claims.source: We found that a majority of spines that were responsive to the sparse noise stimulus also responded to drifting gratings (97%).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: Most spines (89%) had a significant correlation with the network signal.
claims.source: In our population of spines, we found that most spines (89%) had a significant correlation with the network signal.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: All visually responsive spines had a significant correlation with the network signal.
claims.source: This included the visually responsive spines, all of which had a significant correlation with the network signal (see Methods).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: 24% of spines were classified as visually responsive.
claims.source: All spines with time-locked responses to visual stimuli at above chance levels (see Methods) were classified as visually responsive spines (24%; Figure 2B), even though their activity also correlated with the network signal.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: 65% of spines were classified as network-correlated.
claims.source: Spines with activity that correlated with the network signal, but did not have visually-evoked responses, were classified as network-correlated (65%).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: 11% of spines were classified as unclassified.
claims.source: The remainder of spines neither responded to the visual stimuli nor correlated with the network activity, which we refer to as unclassified (11%; Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: Unclassified spines showed no evidence of significant correlations with pupil movement, pupil dilation, or whisker movement above chance.
claims.source: We tested whether these unclassified spines were correlated with other behavioral measures, such as pupil movement, pupil dilation (diameter), and whisker movement, and found no evidence of significant correlations above chance (see Methods).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: There were no significant differences in the average activity in the three groups of spines (network-correlated, visually responsive, unclassified) prior to deprivation.
claims.source: There were no significant differences in the average activity in the three groups of spines prior to deprivation (measured as the area under the curve of the ΔF/F0 fluorescence signal; comparison between network-correlated, visually responsive and unclassified spine activity, one-way ANOVA, p=0.232).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claims.claim: All of the branches measured had all three types of spines (visually responsive, network-correlated, unclassified).
claims.source: All of the branches that we measured had all three types of spines (visually responsive, network-correlated, unclassified).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: The local spatial organization of functional response properties of dendritic spines were not different from chance within individual dendritic branches.
claims.source: Within individual dendritic branches, we found that the local spatial organization of functional response properties (visually responsive, network-correlated, unclassified) of the dendritic spines were not different from chance (Figure 2D–F, see Methods).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: There was no evidence of an increase in the amplitude of the persistent spines identified as visually responsive following deprivation.
claims.source: Consistent with our earlier finding (Figure 2C), we found no evidence of an increase in the amplitude of the persistent spines identified as visually responsive (Figure 3A), or of the persistent unclassified spines (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: There was no evidence of an increase in the amplitude of the persistent unclassified spines following deprivation.
claims.source: Consistent with our earlier finding (Figure 2C), we found no evidence of an increase in the amplitude of the persistent spines identified as visually responsive (Figure 3A), or of the persistent unclassified spines (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: Following deprivation there was an increase in the response amplitude of persistent network-correlated spines.
claims.source: However, following deprivation there was an increase in the response amplitude of persistent network-correlated spines (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: A decrease in the frequency of responses of visually responsive spines was observed over time following deprivation.
claims.source: While the average frequency of responses did not change following deprivation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), we examined if functional groups of spines had changes in response frequency and observed a decrease in the frequency of responses of visually responsive spines over time following deprivation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: A decrease in the integral of activity for visually responsive spines was observed over time following deprivation.
claims.source: When we examined the integral of the activity trace (which combines amplitude and frequency) over time following deprivation, we observed a decrease for visually responsive spines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), no change for unclassified spines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), and an increase for network-correlated spines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: No change in the integral of activity for unclassified spines was observed over time following deprivation.
claims.source: When we examined the integral of the activity trace (which combines amplitude and frequency) over time following deprivation, we observed a decrease for visually responsive spines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), no change for unclassified spines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), and an increase for network-correlated spines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: An increase in the integral of activity for network-correlated spines was observed over time following deprivation.
claims.source: When we examined the integral of the activity trace (which combines amplitude and frequency) over time following deprivation, we observed a decrease for visually responsive spines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), no change for unclassified spines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), and an increase for network-correlated spines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: A strong increase in the fraction of inactive visually responsive spines was found after deprivation.
claims.source: We also found a strong increase in the fraction of inactive visually responsive spines after deprivation.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: The increase in spine loss previously reported following enucleation may include both spines that were visually responsive and network-correlated prior to deprivation.
claims.source: These results suggest that the increase in spine loss previously reported following enucleation (Barnes et al., 2017) may include both spines that were visually responsive and network-correlated prior to deprivation (Figure 3D–F).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings and previous work.

claims.claim: A sizeable fraction of visually responsive spines remains active after visual deprivation.
claims.source: A sizeable fraction of visually responsive spines remains active after visual deprivation (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: Following sensory deprivation, responses to visual stimuli were no longer observed in the visually responsive spines.
claims.source: It is important to note that following sensory deprivation, we no longer observed responses to visual stimuli in the visually responsive spines, since the feedforward input had been permanently removed.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: The responses of the previously categorized visually responsive spines consisted of network responses following deprivation.
claims.source: The responses of the previously categorized visually responsive spines consisted of network responses following deprivation.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: There was no correlation between amplitude and frequency within individual spines in any of the groups (visually responsive, unclassified, network-correlated).
claims.source: There was no correlation between amplitude and frequency within individual spines in any of the groups (Figure 3G–I), again suggesting that frequency decrease does not regulate changes in amplitude within individual spines in this paradigm.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: Frequency decrease does not regulate changes in amplitude within individual spines in this paradigm.
claims.source: There was no correlation between amplitude and frequency within individual spines in any of the groups (Figure 3G–I), again suggesting that frequency decrease does not regulate changes in amplitude within individual spines in this paradigm.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between frequency and amplitude changes.

claims.claim: Network-correlated inputs, and not the identified visually responsive inputs, are homeostatically strengthened following sensory input loss.
claims.source: Overall, these results suggest the network-correlated inputs, and not the identified visually responsive inputs, are homeostatically strengthened following sensory input loss.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claims.claim: The retrosplenial cortex (RSC) receives measurable auditory responsive and visually responsive inputs.
claims.source: To investigate this issue, we used a multimodal brain area – the retrosplenial cortex (RSC) – which receives measurable auditory responsive and visually responsive inputs (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claims.claim: 92% of spines in RSC had activity that was correlated with the network signal.
claims.source: Using the same classification approach as before (Figure 2, see Methods), we found that the activity of 92% of the spines was correlated with the network signal.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: 18.7% of spines in RSC had time-locked responses to visual stimuli.
claims.source: Within this group, a subset of spines had time-locked responses to visual (18.7%) or auditory (15.9%) stimuli (Figure 4A) and the rest correlated only with the network signal (57.4%, Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: 15.9% of spines in RSC had time-locked responses to auditory stimuli.
claims.source: Within this group, a subset of spines had time-locked responses to visual (18.7%) or auditory (15.9%) stimuli (Figure 4A) and the rest correlated only with the network signal (57.4%, Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: 57.4% of spines in RSC correlated only with the network signal.
claims.source: Within this group, a subset of spines had time-locked responses to visual (18.7%) or auditory (15.9%) stimuli (Figure 4A) and the rest correlated only with the network signal (57.4%, Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: 8% of spines in RSC were unclassified (no correlation with the network signal and no sensory-evoked responses).
claims.source: The remaining 8% of spines were unclassified (no correlation with the network signal and no sensory-evoked responses).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: Following reversible visual deprivation via dark exposure for 48 hr, an increase in the average spine response amplitude across the population was observed in RSC.
claims.source: Following reversible visual deprivation via dark exposure for 48 hr (Figure 4B), we observed an increase in the average spine response amplitude across the population.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claims.claim: The increase in average spine response amplitude in RSC following dark exposure was TNF-α-dependent.
claims.source: This response was TNF-α-dependent (Figure 4C), similar to what we observed in visual cortex following enucleation (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claims.claim: In RSC, an increase in the response amplitude of the network-correlated spines was observed following visual deprivation, but not in the visually responsive or unclassified spines.
claims.source: When we examined the changes in the responses of functionally identified spines, we observed an increase in the response amplitude of the network-correlated spines, but not in the visually responsive or unclassified spines (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C), consistent with our results in visual cortex (Figure 2C, Figure 3A–C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: After visual deprivation, the auditory responsive spines did not undergo functional strengthening but maintained their baseline amplitude.
claims.source: We then examined the responses of the auditory responsive spines, which represent an identified non-deprived sensory input. After visual deprivation, the auditory responsive spines did not undergo functional strengthening but maintained their baseline amplitude following visual deprivation (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: Following auditory deprivation, a TNF-α-dependent population increase in spine responses was observed in RSC.
claims.source: To ensure that the strengthening effects that we observed were not exclusive to visual deprivation, we performed a complementary, but separate, experiment where we deprived mice of auditory input through reversible ear plugging for 48 hr and again measured post-deprivation spine responses in the RSC (Figure 4F). We observed a TNF-α-dependent population increase in spine responses (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Following auditory deprivation, network-correlated spines increased their responses, but there was no change in the response strength of either visually responsive or auditory responsive spines.
claims.source: Similar to visual deprivation, network-correlated spines increased their responses following auditory deprivation (Figure 4H–I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F), but there was no change in the response strength of either (non-deprived) visually responsive (Figure 4H) or (deprived) auditory responsive spines (Figure 4I).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: Increases in spine response amplitude predominantly occur in the spines whose activity correlated with the network signal and not in the spines which are responsive to the non-deprived or deprived sensory stimulation.
claims.source: Together, these data suggest that increases in spine response amplitude predominantly occur in the spines whose activity correlated with the network signal and not in the spines which are responsive to the non-deprived or deprived sensory stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Following visual deprivation, there is a homeostatic increase in the cellular visually-evoked responses relative to baseline.
claims.source: Previous work has shown that following visual deprivation, there is a homeostatic increase in the cellular visually-evoked responses relative to baseline (Mrsic-Flogel et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: This homeostatic response is hypothesized to occur through a presumed strengthening of the spared visual inputs.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Following visual deprivation via dark exposure, the global dendritic responses in RSC to both visual and auditory stimulation were increased when compared with baseline measurements.
claims.source: We found that following visual deprivation via dark exposure, the global dendritic responses in RSC to both visual and auditory stimulation were increased when compared with baseline measurements (Figure 4J), consistent with past results (Mrsic-Flogel et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, consistent with previous work.

claims.claim: Neither the visually responsive nor auditory responsive spines increased their responses to the same respective stimuli following visual deprivation.
claims.source: This was despite the fact that neither the visually responsive nor auditory responsive spines increased their responses to the same respective stimuli (Figure 4D–E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: Both the global visually-evoked responses and individual visually responsive spines maintained their visual tuning before and after deprivation at levels comparable to control.
claims.source: Both the global visually-evoked responses and individual visually responsive spines maintained their visual tuning before and after deprivation at levels comparable to control (Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).

claims.claim: Increases in global dendritic responses after deprivation were uncorrelated with the changes in visually-evoked spine responses on those dendrites.

claims.claim: It is unlikely that increases in global dendritic responses were driven by increases in the strength of visually-evoked spine responses.
claims.source: Increases in global dendritic responses after deprivation were uncorrelated with the changes in visually-evoked spine responses on those dendrites, making it unlikely that increases in global dendritic responses were driven by increases in the strength of visually-evoked spine responses (Figure 4K).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between global dendritic responses and visually-evoked spine responses.

claims.claim: There was no relationship within a dendrite between changes in global dendritic responses and auditory-evoked spine responses.
claims.source: There was also no relationship within a dendrite between changes in global dendritic responses and auditory-evoked spine responses (Figure 4L).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: Increases in global dendritic responses were correlated with an increase in the network-correlated spine activity on the same dendrites.
claims.source: Conversely, increases in global dendritic responses were correlated with an increase in the network-correlated spine activity on the same dendrites (Figure 4M).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: Increases in sensory-evoked global dendritic responses are unlikely to result from increases in the response strength of the identified sensory responsive inputs.
claims.source: Our results suggest that increases in sensory-evoked global dendritic responses are unlikely to result from increases in the response strength of the identified sensory responsive inputs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claims.claim: A TNF-α-dependent increase in the functional responses of dendritic spines in awake mice was observed following sensory deprivation.
claims.source: Here, we report a TNF-α-dependent increase in the functional responses of dendritic spines in awake mice following sensory deprivation.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Dendritic spines whose activity is correlated with the network signal are strengthened following sensory deprivation, but spines identified as sensory responsive are not.
claims.source: Surprisingly, when we examine the functional properties of spines that undergo strengthening, we find dendritic spines whose activity is correlated with the network signal are strengthened, but spines identified as sensory responsive are not.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the experimental data.

claims.claim: The strengthening of network-correlated spines occurs over a similar time course and magnitude in both visual cortex and RSC and in response to different deprivation paradigms.
claims.source: This strengthening of network-correlated spines occurs over a similar time course and magnitude in both visual cortex and RSC and in response to different deprivation paradigms.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the experimental data.

claims.claim: A homeostatic increase in global sensory-evoked responses was observed following sensory deprivation, despite the fact that there was no increase in responses of sensory responsive spines.

claims.evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the experimental data.

claims.claim: The global increase in sensory-evoked responses is correlated with an increase in the response strength of network-correlated spines on those branches, but not of identified sensory responsive spines.
claims.source: This global increase is correlated with an increase in the response strength of network-correlated spines on those branches, but not of identified sensory responsive spines.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the experimental data.

claims.claim: In vivo synaptic homeostasis during adulthood occurs in a functional subset of inputs, specifically those correlated only with network activity, rather than the identified sensory responsive inputs that are thought to drive sensory processing.
claims.source: Our findings suggest that in vivo synaptic homeostasis during adulthood occurs in a functional subset of inputs, specifically those correlated only with network activity, rather than the identified sensory responsive inputs that are thought to drive sensory processing.

claims.claim: The homeostatic increase in sensory-evoked responses observed after deprivation in adult mice is not associated with increases in the response strength of identified sensory responsive inputs.
claims.source: Our results suggest that the homeostatic increase in sensory-evoked responses observed after deprivation in adult mice is not associated with increases in the response strength of identified sensory responsive inputs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claims.claim: A correlation was observed between increases in global sensory-evoked activity levels and increases in the functional response strength of network-correlated spines.
claims.source: Instead, we observe a correlation between increases in global sensory-evoked activity levels and increases in the functional response strength of network-correlated spines.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: The strengthened network connections may serve to amplify intrinsic activity, keeping cells closer to the threshold for action potential generation and thereby making incoming sensory responsive inputs more likely to elicit the observed sensory-evoked increases in post-synaptic activity.

claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed findings.

claims.claim: Previous work has shown that homeostatic recovery at the level of small networks of cells is mediated by increases in the intrinsic network activity.

claims.claim: Intrinsic network activity is amplified within interconnected neural ensembles.

claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The amplification of network activity through a strengthening of network connections may underlie rebalancing of activity in the cortex following sensory deprivation affecting network activity.

claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and previous work.

claims.claim: Amplification of network activity provides a mechanism during adulthood by which overall activity can be modulated through the network inputs, without altering the identified sensory inputs and the established circuits thought to drive sensory processing.
claims.source: This provides a mechanism during adulthood by which overall activity can be modulated through the network inputs, without altering the identified sensory inputs and the established circuits thought to drive sensory processing.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

results.result: The manuscript establishes the background and motivation for studying homeostatic plasticity in adult animals. Homeostatic regulation is essential for stable neuronal function and occurs through various mechanisms, but the functional properties of synapses involved in homeostasis during adulthood remain unknown, particularly regarding which synaptic subsets undergo homeostatic changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C10-C15 establish well-supported background from the literature. These claims cite appropriate prior work and accurately represent established knowledge about homeostatic plasticity mechanisms and their importance. The identification of a knowledge gap (C3) regarding functional properties of homeostatically regulated synapses is well-motivated.

results.result: The study employed longitudinal two-photon calcium imaging of dendritic spines in awake adult mice to measure functional responses before and after sensory deprivation. The methodology included multiple deprivation paradigms (monocular enucleation, dark exposure, auditory deprivation) and TNF-α inhibition experiments across visual cortex and retrosplenial cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C19-C20, and C110-C124 describe comprehensive and well-documented experimental methods. The approach is appropriate for addressing the research question, with adequate sample sizes (43 mice, 5858 spines), proper controls, ethical approval, and established imaging techniques. The methods are sufficiently detailed for reproducibility.

results.result: Following monocular deprivation, approximately 20% of spines became inactive at 12 hours with recovery over time, while persistent spines showed TNF-α-dependent increases in response amplitude. Changes in spine amplitude were independent of changes in response frequency within individual spines.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C28 present clear experimental findings with appropriate statistical analysis and controls. The TNF-α dependence is demonstrated through pharmacological blockade (C24-C25), and the lack of correlation between frequency and amplitude changes (C27-C28) is properly quantified. Results are consistent with prior work (C21) and supported by Figure 1.

results.result: Dendritic spines were functionally classified into three groups: visually responsive (24%), network-correlated (65%), and unclassified (11%). All visually responsive spines also correlated with network activity. The three spine types showed no spatial clustering on dendritic branches and had similar baseline activity levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C41 and C125-C130 describe a rigorous classification scheme with appropriate statistical thresholds and validation. The false positive rate analysis (C129) and testing for correlations with other behavioral variables (C38, C130) strengthen the classification. The spatial analysis (C41) and baseline activity comparison (C39) provide important controls. Methods are clearly described and reproducible.

results.result: Following sensory deprivation in visual cortex, network-correlated spines showed increased response amplitudes while visually responsive and unclassified spines did not. Visually responsive spines showed decreased frequency and overall activity, with many becoming inactive. The strengthening was specific to network-correlated inputs, not sensory responsive inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C56 present the core finding with strong experimental support. The inverse relationship between visual responsiveness and strengthening (C30) is clearly demonstrated. The differential effects on the three spine classes (C42-C48) are well-documented with appropriate statistics and controls. The lack of correlation between frequency and amplitude changes within spines (C54-C55) is properly analyzed. Figure 3 provides clear visual support.

results.result: In retrosplenial cortex (RSC), a multimodal area receiving both visual and auditory inputs, network-correlated spines (57.4%) showed TNF-α-dependent strengthening following either visual or auditory deprivation. Neither deprived sensory inputs (visual or auditory) nor non-deprived sensory inputs showed strengthening, confirming that homeostatic changes target network-correlated rather than sensory-responsive inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C69 provide critical validation of the main finding in a different brain region and with multiple sensory modalities. The use of RSC allows testing of both deprived and non-deprived sensory inputs (C66, C68), which is a strong experimental design. The consistency across visual and auditory deprivation paradigms (C67-C68) and the TNF-α dependence (C64, C67) strengthen the conclusions. The results are well-supported by Figure 4.

results.result: Following visual deprivation, global dendritic responses to both visual and auditory stimuli increased homeostatically, despite no strengthening of individual sensory-responsive spines. The increase in global responses correlated with strengthening of network-correlated spines on the same dendrites, not with changes in sensory-responsive spines, suggesting global responses are driven by network-correlated inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C79 address a critical question about the relationship between spine-level and cellular-level responses. The finding that global responses increase (C72) despite no strengthening of sensory spines (C73) is paradoxical but well-documented. The correlation analysis (C75, C77, C78) appropriately tests the relationship between global and spine-specific changes. The maintenance of visual tuning (C74) provides an important control. This reconciles the current findings with prior literature (C70-C71).

results.result: The study demonstrates that in vivo synaptic homeostasis in adult mice occurs selectively in network-correlated inputs rather than sensory-responsive inputs. This selective strengthening occurs across multiple brain regions and deprivation paradigms, is TNF-α-dependent, and correlates with homeostatic increases in global sensory-evoked responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C87 summarize the main findings, which are well-supported by the experimental data. The consistency across brain regions (visual cortex and RSC), sensory modalities (visual and auditory), and deprivation paradigms (enucleation, dark exposure, ear plugging) provides strong evidence. The TNF-α dependence is clearly demonstrated. The correlation between network-correlated spine strengthening and global response increases (C87) is properly quantified.

results.result: The authors propose that strengthened network connections amplify intrinsic activity, bringing cells closer to action potential threshold and thereby increasing responses to sensory inputs without altering the sensory inputs themselves. This mechanism allows homeostatic regulation while preserving established sensory processing circuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C92 present a mechanistic interpretation supported by the data and prior literature (C89-C90). The proposed mechanism (C88) is speculative but reasonable given the experimental findings. The interpretation that this preserves sensory processing circuits (C92) is logical and consistent with the observation that sensory tuning is maintained (C74). However, this remains a proposed mechanism requiring further direct testing.

results.result: The functional strengthening of network-correlated spines is TNF-α-dependent. Prior work shows TNF-α facilitates AMPAR insertion and synaptic strengthening through GRIP1, selectively affecting homeostatic but not Hebbian plasticity, which may explain the selective strengthening observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C98 appropriately cite prior literature on TNF-α mechanisms. The TNF-α dependence is experimentally demonstrated in the current study (C93), and the mechanistic interpretation based on prior work (C94-C98) is reasonable. The selective action of TNF-α on AMPARs but not NMDARs (C95) and on homeostatic but not Hebbian plasticity (C96) provides a plausible molecular basis for the observed selectivity.

results.result: Following sensory deprivation, a fraction of visually responsive spines become inactive, potentially through spine loss. However, many sensory-responsive spines remain active without strengthening, regardless of whether they encode deprived or non-deprived inputs. This preservation may underlie the stability of visual tuning observed after deprivation.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C105 describe the fate of sensory-responsive spines with appropriate caveats. The observation that sensory spines don't strengthen (C103-C104) is well-documented. The inference about spine loss (C101-C102) is appropriately qualified as it relies on prior structural imaging work. The connection to tuning stability (C105) is reasonable and supported by the data showing maintained tuning (C74).

results.result: By homeostatically regulating network-correlated inputs rather than sensory inputs, the system maintains the dynamic range of sensory-responsive inputs and preserves feedforward sensory processing circuits. This avoids potential saturation of sensory inputs that could occur with multiplicative scaling and would reduce information processing capacity.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C109 present a functional interpretation of the findings, supported by prior theoretical work (C107-C108). The argument that selective regulation of network inputs preserves sensory processing (C106, C109) is logical and consistent with the data. The concern about saturation (C107-C108) is appropriately cited from prior work. This provides a compelling functional rationale for the observed selectivity.

results.result: The network signal measured in this study reflects intrinsic cortical activity, potentially including intracortical connections and contextual inputs, but not locomotion-related activity. The interpretation of inactive spines and the nature of dendritic signals are appropriately qualified with methodological limitations.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C18 and C132-C135 provide important context and caveats. The characterization of the network signal (C16-C18) is supported by appropriate citations. The clarifications about experimental conditions (C133) and methodological limitations (C134-C135) are important for proper interpretation. The acknowledgment that dendritic signals likely reflect back-propagating action potentials (C132) is appropriately cited.
